paragraphs.title: A Call to Song and Shofar Blasts at the Festival

easy.explanation: The psalm begins by calling people to sing aloud and make a joyful noise unto God.
easy.q: What does the psalm call people to do at the beginning?

easy.explanation: The passage names the timbrel, the pleasant harp, and the psaltery.
easy.q: Which instruments are mentioned in these verses?

easy.explanation: Verse 3 says, “Blow up the trumpet in the new moon.”
easy.q: What instrument are the people told to blow?

answers: In the new moon and at the solemn feast day
medium.explanation: The trumpet was to be blown in the new moon and at the appointed feast.
medium.q: When were the people told to blow the trumpet?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to God, who is called “our strength.”
medium.q: What does “our strength” refer to in verse 1?

answers: They move from musical praise to trumpet blowing at the feast
They tell how enemies were defeated
medium.explanation: The verses call for singing, joyful noise, instruments, and trumpet blowing during the feast.

answers: It marks the appointed feast and Israel’s statute
It describes Israel’s suffering in Egypt
challenge.explanation: The trumpet is connected with the new moon, the solemn feast day, and a statute for Israel.
challenge.q: What role does the trumpet have in this passage?

answers: Praise is expressed through singing, joyful noise, and instruments at the feast
Praise must be whispered without instruments
The feast is presented as a time without singing
challenge.explanation: The passage joins the feast with joyful praise and musical celebration.
challenge.q: What connection is made between praise and the feast?

answers: The passage moves from praise to a specific statute concerning the trumpet
It moves from warning to exile
It moves from enemies to food
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with general praise and ends by identifying the feast observance as a statute and law.

paragraphs.title: Remembering God’s Kindness to Joseph and Israel

easy.explanation: The verse says, “I removed his shoulder from the burden.”
easy.q: What did God remove from the person described in verse 6?

easy.explanation: His hands were delivered from the pots.
easy.q: What were his hands delivered from?

answers: He gave them to their enemies
easy.explanation: God says, “Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee.”
easy.q: What did God do when His people called in trouble?

answers: God freed His people from burdens and trouble
God taught them a foreign language
medium.explanation: The passage describes release from burdens and deliverance in trouble.
medium.q: What kind of kindness is described in verses 6–7?

medium.explanation: The phrase means that God rescued the one who called to Him in trouble.
medium.q: What does “I delivered thee” mean in context?

answers: Release from labor and rescue in trouble
Rescue from hunger and war only
Escape from the feast and the music
medium.explanation: The passage speaks of removing a burden and delivering someone who called in trouble.
medium.q: Which two situations of help are mentioned?

answers: Both are associated with God’s acts of deliverance
Both are described as enemies of God
Both are presented as worshipers of strange gods
challenge.explanation: The surrounding passage recalls God’s saving care for Joseph and Israel.
challenge.q: How are Joseph and Israel connected with God’s kindness in the larger passage?

answers: It shows that God’s help was given during a time of testing
It removes the connection with Egypt
challenge.explanation: Meribah recalls a difficult testing situation in which God answered His people.
challenge.q: What does the reference to “the waters of Meribah” add to the passage?

answers: The people called in trouble, and God answered and delivered them
The people were silent, and God hid them
The people celebrated, and God stopped the singing
challenge.explanation: The passage directly connects calling in trouble with God’s answer and deliverance.
challenge.q: What relationship appears between calling and God’s response?

paragraphs.title: Warning Against Disobedience and Foreign Worship

easy.explanation: God says, “Hear, O my people,” and then addresses Israel.
The passage forbids having a strange god and worshiping any strange god.
easy.q: What were the people forbidden to have or worship?

easy.explanation: Verse 11 says, “My people would not hearken to my voice.”
easy.q: What did God’s people refuse to do?

answers: To remind them of His deliverance and their relationship with Him
To explain the origin of the instruments
To explain where wheat came from
medium.explanation: The Exodus reminds Israel of God’s saving favor and their obligation to listen to Him.
medium.q: Why does God remind Israel that He brought them out of Egypt?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the desires of their own disobedient hearts.
medium.q: What does “their own hearts’ lust” mean in this context?

answers: God gave them over to their own desires and counsels
medium.explanation: God says, “So I gave them up unto their own hearts’ lust.”
medium.q: What happened because the people would not listen?

answers: God’s command to listen versus the people’s refusal
challenge.explanation: God calls Israel to hear Him, but the people refuse to hearken to His voice.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verses 9–13?

answers: Both are departures from God’s way
They are unrelated in the passage
challenge.explanation: The warning against strange gods appears alongside the command to listen to God.
challenge.q: How are foreign worship and disobedience related in the passage?

answers: Refusing God leads the people to follow their own desires and counsel
Refusing God leads immediately to abundance
Refusing God leads to blowing the trumpet
challenge.explanation: After the people refuse to listen, God gives them over to their own hearts and counsels.
challenge.q: What does the movement from command to consequence show?

paragraphs.title: Victory and Abundance for Those Who Obey God

easy.explanation: God says, “Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways!”
easy.q: What does God wish Israel would do?

easy.explanation: God says He would soon have subdued their enemies.
easy.q: What would happen to Israel’s enemies if Israel obeyed God?

answers: The finest of the wheat and honey from the rock
easy.explanation: The final verse mentions the finest wheat and honey out of the rock.
easy.q: What food is mentioned as a blessing?

answers: That Israel would hearken to God and walk in His ways
That Israel would worship a strange god
medium.explanation: God’s promise is presented in connection with Israel listening to Him and walking in His ways.
medium.q: What is the condition connected with God’s promised victory?

medium.explanation: The word “soon” indicates that God would quickly subdue Israel’s enemies.
medium.q: What does “I should soon have subdued” indicate?

answers: Walking in God’s ways leads to victory and nourishing provision
Foreign worship leads to wheat and honey
medium.explanation: The passage presents obedience as the path to subdued enemies and abundant food.
medium.q: What cause-and-effect sequence appears in these verses?

answers: Both are presented as blessings God would give His obedient people
challenge.explanation: The ending promises both protection from enemies and rich nourishment.
challenge.q: How are victory and abundance related at the end of the psalm?

answers: God’s provision would be rich and satisfying
The people would have no food
Honey was used as an instrument
challenge.explanation: The language of satisfaction and honey presents abundant, nourishing provision.
challenge.q: What does “with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee” suggest?

answers: It shows the blessing that could come if Israel listened to God
It continues describing only Israel’s refusal
It cancels the command to listen
challenge.explanation: After describing disobedience, the psalm presents the blessings available through listening and walking in God’s ways.
challenge.q: How does the ending relate to the warning in the preceding verses?
